events.title: Lex Ogulnia: plebeians admitted to the priestly colleges
events.summary: The tribunes Q. and Cn. Ogulnius carried a law raising the pontiffs from four to eight and the augurs from four to nine, the new places reserved for plebeians.
events.detail: With this the last major patrician monopoly fell, apart from a few archaic priesthoods (rex sacrorum, the major flamines, the Salii) that stayed patrician. Livy gives Appius Claudius Caecus a speech against it and P. Decius Mus a speech for it. Control of the calendar, auspices and sacral law now passed to a mixed patricio-plebeian nobility; the first plebeian pontifex maximus, Ti. Coruncanius, followed c. 254.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 90-130
Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome I (1998) 64-68

events.title: Lex Valeria de provocatione (300)
events.summary: The consul M. Valerius Corvus carried a law forbidding magistrates to flog or execute a citizen who appealed to the people; Livy calls it the third such law, 'always brought by the same family'.
events.detail: Livy remarks that the only sanction was that violation would be 'improbe factum', a wicked act, showing how much early Roman law relied on social pressure. Most scholars regard this as the first historical lex de provocatione, the 509 and 449 laws being retrojections.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 130-145
Lintott, 'Provocatio', ANRW I.2 (1972)

events.title: Colony at Narnia; last tribes of the century
events.summary: After a long siege of the Umbrian town of Nequinum, Rome refounded it as the Latin colony of Narnia on a cliff above the Nar gorge, and created the tribes Aniensis and Teretina (33 in all).
events.detail: Narnia controlled the route into Umbria later followed by the Via Flaminia (220). The same year, Polybius says, Gauls joined by Etruscans plundered Roman territory and returned home unscathed.

events.title: Alliance with the Lucanians; outbreak of the Third Samnite War
events.summary: Lucanian envoys asked Rome for protection against a Samnite invasion and gave hostages; Rome ordered the Samnites out of Lucania, they refused, and the fetials declared war.
events.detail: The war rapidly widened into a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls, the greatest challenge Rome had yet faced in Italy.

events.title: Campaign of L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus
events.summary: The epitaph on Scipio Barbatus' sarcophagus in the Tomb of the Scipios claims he 'took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium, subdued all Lucania and brought back hostages'; Livy instead places the consul of 298 in Etruria fighting near Volaterrae.
events.detail: The peperino sarcophagus, now in the Vatican, with its Saturnian verse inscription (CIL I2 6-7) is the earliest substantial Roman elogium and a rare documentary check on Livy, revealing family claims and annalistic confusion side by side. Barbatus' son L. Scipio (cos. 259) took Corsica.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 154-170
Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni', Dialoghi di Archeologia 6 (1972)

events.title: Battle near Tifernum
events.summary: Q. Fabius Rullianus, consul for the fourth time, defeated a Samnite army that had tried to ambush him in a valley near Tifernum, while his colleague P. Decius Mus beat the Apulians at Maleventum.
events.detail: Livy offers the usual inflated casualty figures (3,400 killed, 830 captured, 23 standards). The location of Tifernum in Samnium (perhaps the Matese massif or the upper Biferno) is uncertain.

events.title: Gellius Egnatius forms the anti-Roman coalition
events.summary: The Samnite leader Gellius Egnatius led an army north through the Apennines into Etruria and organised a grand coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls against Rome.
events.detail: The strategic boldness of the plan is clear even through Livy's narrative: by uniting Rome's enemies north of the Tiber with the Samnites, Egnatius aimed to force Rome to fight on one decisive field against superior numbers. The Roman response was to raise perhaps six legions and arm freedmen.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 263-268

events.title: Appius Claudius Caecus vows the Temple of Bellona
events.summary: In a battle against Etruscans and Samnites Appius Claudius vowed a temple to Bellona, later built near the Circus Flaminius outside the pomerium; its anniversary was 3 June.
events.detail: Before the temple stood the columna bellica, over which the fetial hurled a spear into a plot deemed 'enemy territory' to declare war on distant foes; the Senate met there to receive returning generals and foreign envoys. Appius' elogium credits him with the vow.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: The Ogulnii set up the she-wolf and twins
events.summary: The curule aediles Cn. and Q. Ogulnius, using fines from moneylenders, set up statues of the infant Romulus and Remus under the she-wolf at the Ficus Ruminalis, placed bronze thresholds and vessels on the Capitol, and paved the road from the Porta Capena to the temple of Mars.
events.detail: The first securely dated monument of the twins legend, which appears on Romano-Campanian silver didrachms c. 269. (The Capitoline Wolf bronze, long thought Etruscan, has been radiocarbon-dated to the Middle Ages, and the twins were added in the Renaissance.) The same year a patrician woman, Verginia, excluded from the cult of Pudicitia Patricia for marrying a plebeian, founded an altar of Pudicitia Plebeia in her house on the Vicus Longus.
events.locName: Ficus Ruminalis by the Lupercal, Rome
scholarship: Wiseman, Remus: A Roman Myth (1995)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 250-270

events.title: Citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa
events.summary: Two small coastal citizen colonies of 300 families each were planted at Minturnae on the Liris mouth and at Sinuessa on the Massic coast, in former Ausonian land, though recruits were hard to find.
events.detail: Minturnae's castrum-style rectangular fort (c. 2.5 ha) is a classic example of the 'coloniae maritimae'; Marius hid in its marshes in 88.

events.title: Destruction of a Roman legion near Camerinum
events.summary: Before Sentinum, the Senones (with Samnites) annihilated a Roman legion under the propraetor L. Cornelius Scipio; Polybius places it near Camerinum, Livy near Clusium, and Livy notes some sources said the Gauls rode off with heads on their spears and hanging from their horses' chests.
events.detail: The disaster revealed the size of the coalition and caused the Romans to concentrate both consuls, Fabius and Decius, with four legions in Umbria.

sides.strength: one legion under L. Cornelius Scipio

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 280-300

events.title: Battle of Sentinum
events.summary: At Sentinum in Umbria the consuls Q. Fabius Rullianus and P. Decius Mus, with four legions and as many allies, defeated the Samnites under Gellius Egnatius and the Senonian Gauls; when Gallic chariots broke the Roman left, Decius devoted himself like his father, and the line held.
events.detail: Livy's figures (25,000 enemy dead, 8,000 captured; Romans 8,700 killed) are among the more plausible in his narrative. Duris of Samos, a contemporary, wrote that 100,000 died, the first Roman battle reported in a Greek historian. Fabius' wing wore down the Samnites, then took the Gauls in the rear; Gellius Egnatius fell. Diversionary attacks on Etruria had already drawn the Etruscans and Umbrians home. Fabius vowed a temple to Jupiter Victor. Sentinum decided the fate of Italy: the coalition never re-formed, and within 25 years Rome controlled the peninsula.

battle.significance: Decisive battle for the mastery of Italy; collapse of the Samnite-Gallic-Etruscan coalition.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 285-345
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 268-270
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 359-362

events.title: Temple of Venus Obsequens built from fines on adulteresses
events.summary: Q. Fabius Gurges as curule aedile fined matrons convicted of adultery (stuprum) and used the money to build a temple of Venus Obsequens near the Circus Maximus, Rome's first temple of Venus.
events.detail: The aedile's role in policing sexual morality and funding public buildings from fines is typical of the period (cf. the Ogulnii, 296). The same year the Fasti record plague and prodigies.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Victoria on the Palatine
events.summary: L. Postumius Megellus dedicated the temple of Victory on the Palatine, built as aedile from fines; in 204 the black stone of Magna Mater was housed there until her own temple was ready next door.
events.detail: The cult of the personified goddess Victoria reflects Hellenistic influence (Nike) at the height of the Samnite wars. Remains on the south-west Palatine have been identified.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Battle of Aquilonia
events.summary: The consul L. Papirius Cursor (son of the dictator) crushed the Samnite 'linen legion' at Aquilonia, while his colleague Sp. Carvilius took Cominium; the Samnites had sworn its 16,000 picked men by gruesome oaths in a linen-roofed enclosure, executing those who refused.
events.detail: When the sacred chickens would not eat, the pullarius lied that the omens were favourable; Papirius said the falsehood fell on the reporter's head, and the man was killed by a stray javelin at the start of the battle. Papirius vowed a cup of mead to Jupiter Victor if he won. Livy's account of the Samnite oath (an old priest named Ovius Paccius, a ritual from ancient linen books) is consistent with Oscan religious practice. Papirius' triumph displayed 2,533,000 pounds of bronze from the sale of captives and 1,830 pounds of silver. The site is disputed (Monte Vairano near Campobasso, or near Lacedonia).

battle.significance: Final great field battle of the Samnite wars.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 380-440
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 182-186

events.title: Temple of Quirinus and Rome's first sundial
events.summary: L. Papirius Cursor dedicated the temple of Quirinus vowed by his father and decorated it with Samnite spoils; Pliny, citing Fabius Vestalis, says he set up the first sundial in Rome there.
events.detail: Pliny records an alternative tradition that the first sundial was brought from Catana in Sicily by M'. Valerius Messalla in 263, wrongly calibrated for Rome's latitude yet used for 99 years. The temple on the Quirinal was rebuilt by Augustus with 76 columns.

events.title: Census of 293: 262,321 citizens
events.summary: Livy records 262,321 citizens counted in the census of 293, the first of the mid-Republican figures generally treated as broadly reliable (adult males, including cives sine suffragio).
events.detail: Later figures: 287,222 (280/279), 271,224 (275), 292,234 (265). The dip after the Pyrrhic war suggests real losses. Rome's citizen manpower, plus the obligation of Latin and allied communities to send troops, gave it a military reserve of several hundred thousand by 225 (Polybius 2.24).
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 BC - AD 14 (1971) 13-14
Scheidel, 'Human mobility in Roman Italy I', JRS 94 (2004)

events.title: Aesculapius brought from Epidaurus to the Tiber Island
events.summary: After a three-year plague and consultation of the Sibylline Books (293), envoys under Q. Ogulnius sailed to Epidaurus; a sacred snake boarded their ship and, at Rome, slipped overboard onto the Tiber Island, where a temple to Aesculapius was dedicated on 1 January.
events.detail: The island sanctuary became Rome's healing centre: sick slaves abandoned there were declared free by Claudius if they recovered. In the 1st century BC the island was faced with travertine in the shape of a ship, with a carved snake-and-staff relief still visible at its prow. The episode marks the culmination of the 4th-3rd century importation of Greek cults.
scholarship: Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome I (1998) 69-70

events.title: Execution of Gavius Pontius
events.summary: Q. Fabius Gurges, after a defeat retrieved with help from his father Rullianus as legate, beat the Samnites and led the captured C. Pontius in his triumph; Pontius, probably the Caudine victor (or his son), was then beheaded.
events.detail: Known only from the Livian epitome and late sources, the execution became a stock example of Roman ruthlessness, criticised as unworthy by later writers. Rullianus rode as legate beside his son's chariot.
events.debate: Whether the executed Pontius is the Caudine commander.

events.title: Latin colony at Venusia
events.summary: Rome founded at Venusia, on the border of Samnium, Apulia and Lucania, a Latin colony that Dionysius says numbered 20,000 colonists, the largest ever, splitting the Samnites from their southern neighbours.
events.detail: The figure may include families. Venusia controlled the Ofanto valley route to Tarentum; it sheltered survivors of Cannae in 216 and was the birthplace of Horace. The consul L. Postumius Megellus was later prosecuted for using his soldiers to clear his own estates.

events.title: Manius Curius conquers the Sabines and Praetuttii
events.summary: The consul M'. Curius Dentatus overran the Sabine country and the Praetuttii to the Adriatic in a single campaign; the Sabines received citizenship without vote (full citizenship in 268), and Rome's territory now crossed Italy from sea to sea.
events.detail: Curius allegedly boasted he had taken so much land that it would have been a desert, and so many men that they would have starved, had he not taken both. He refused more than the seven iugera allotted to each settler, saying a man not content with seven iugera was a dangerous citizen. Peace was concluded with the Samnites the same year, ending the Third Samnite War.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 334-335

events.title: Curius drains the Lacus Velinus (Cascata delle Marmore)
events.summary: Curius Dentatus cut a channel through the travertine sill at Marmore to drain the Lacus Velinus near Reate into the Nar, creating the artificial waterfalls still known as the Cascata delle Marmore and reclaiming the plain of Rosea.
events.detail: The diversion caused centuries of litigation between Reate and Interamna (Terni) over flooding; Cicero represented Reate before a commission in 54 BC. Some date the work to Curius' censorship of 272.

events.title: Latin colony at Hadria
events.summary: Hadria (Atri) in Praetuttian territory was made a Latin colony near the Adriatic, consolidating Curius' conquests; Castrum Novum on the coast may date from the same years.
events.detail: Hadria later minted its own heavy cast bronze (aes grave) with the legend HAT, and was the ancestral home of the emperor Hadrian's family.

events.title: Beginnings of Roman coinage: aes grave and the tresviri monetales
events.summary: The board of three moneyers (tresviri aere argento auro flando feriundo) is traditionally dated c. 289, around the time Rome began casting heavy bronze coins (aes grave) on a libral standard, after centuries of using raw bronze by weight (aes rude) and cast bars (aes signatum).
events.detail: The first Roman silver didrachms, with the legend ROMANO and types such as Mars/horse head, were struck c. 310-300 (Crawford dates the first to c. 280), probably at Neapolis or another Campanian mint, for use in the south. A Pomponius passage in the Digest dates the moneyers to the same reform as the tresviri capitales (c. 290). Coinage at Rome was thus a by-product of conquest and contact with the Greek south, not an archaic institution.
events.locName: Rome (mint by the temple of Juno Moneta, Arx)
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) 35-46
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987) 1-15
events.debate: Exact date of the first moneyers and coins.

events.title: Mamertines seize Messana
events.summary: Campanian mercenaries discharged after Agathocles' death, calling themselves Mamertini ('sons of Mars'), were admitted to Messana as guests, massacred or expelled the men, took their wives and property, and made the city a base for raiding north-east Sicily.
events.detail: Their appeal to Rome (and to Carthage) in 264 against Hiero II of Syracuse triggered the First Punic War. Oscan-language coins of the Mamertines (legend MAMERTINΩN) and inscriptions survive.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 52-53
tags: road to the First Punic War

events.title: Lex Hortensia and the last secession of the plebs
events.summary: After a debt crisis drove the plebs to secede to the Janiculum, the plebeian dictator Q. Hortensius carried a law making plebiscites binding on the whole Roman people without further sanction; the concilium plebis became Rome's main legislative body.
events.detail: The law is often called the formal end of the Struggle of the Orders. Pliny adds that it made the nundinae (market days) court days (fasti), so country people coming to market could settle lawsuits. Hortensius died in office. Most later Republican legislation, from the lex Aquilia (c. 286) to the Gracchan laws, passed as plebiscites. Paradoxically, the 'victory' integrated tribunes into the senatorial governing class, the arrangement that held until 133. Our sources are thin: the relevant books of Livy are lost and only the Periochae, Pliny and Gellius (citing the jurist Laelius Felix) survive.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 341-344
Hölkeskamp, Die Entstehung der Nobilität (1987)
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 349-350
tags: end of the Struggle of the Orders

events.title: Battle of Arretium
events.summary: Senones, joined by Etruscans, besieged Rome's ally Arretium; the relieving army was destroyed and the praetor (or consul) L. Caecilius Metellus Denter killed with 13,000 men. Roman envoys sent to the Senones about prisoners were murdered.
events.detail: Polybius dates it ten years after Sentinum; Livy's epitome places it in 283 and Orosius gives the figure of 13,000 dead and 7 military tribunes. M'. Curius Dentatus, as replacement, then ravaged the Senonian lands.

battle.significance: Provokes the Roman destruction of the Senones.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 187-188
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)
events.debate: Year 284 or 283; Metellus praetor or consul.

events.title: Expulsion of the Senones; colony at Sena Gallica
events.summary: Rome invaded the ager Gallicus, killed or expelled the Senones, and planted a citizen colony at Sena Gallica on the Adriatic coast, the first Roman colony on Gallic land.
events.detail: Polybius says the Romans 'drove out the Senones and became masters of their country'. The ager Gallicus remained public land until C. Flaminius distributed it in 232, a step Polybius saw as a cause of the great Gallic war of 225.
events.locName: Sena Gallica (Senigallia) and the ager Gallicus

events.title: Second battle of Lake Vadimon
events.summary: Alarmed by the fate of the Senones, the Boii joined the Etruscans and marched on Rome; the consul P. Cornelius Dolabella annihilated them at Lake Vadimon, where, Polybius says, most of the Etruscans were cut down and very few Boii escaped.
events.detail: Pliny, citing the same lake, describes its floating islands. The victory ended the Etruscan cities' capacity for coordinated resistance.

sides.losses: most Etruscans killed; few Boii escaped

events.title: Battle near Populonia
events.summary: The Boii, with Etruscans, raised another army of young men the following year and were defeated again; they then sued for peace, which they kept for 45 years.
events.detail: Polybius gives no location; later accounts (Dio/Zonaras) place a defeat of Etruscans and Gauls near Populonia, the Etruscan iron-smelting port opposite Elba, under Q. Aemilius Papus.

sides.strength: consular army of Q. Aemilius Papus

battle.significance: Peace with the Boii for 45 years.

events.title: Fabricius relieves Thurii
events.summary: Thurii, besieged by the Lucanians and Bruttians, appealed to Rome rather than Tarentum; the consul C. Fabricius Luscinus defeated the besiegers, and Rome garrisoned Thurii, Locri, Rhegium and Croton.
events.detail: The Thurians set up a statue and a golden crown for Fabricius. Rome's emergence as protector of Greek cities in the Gulf of Tarentum, against the Lacinian treaty, alarmed Tarentum.

battle.significance: Rome intervenes among the Italiote Greeks.

events.title: Tarentum attacks a Roman squadron and insults Rome's envoy
events.summary: Ten Roman ships under the duumvir L. Valerius sailed into the Gulf of Tarentum; the Tarentines, watching in their theatre, attacked, sank four and killed the commander, then expelled the Roman garrison from Thurii. When L. Postumius Megellus came to demand redress, his Greek was mocked and a drunk soiled his toga; he said the stain would be washed out in blood.
events.detail: The theatre scene and the toga story are later embellishments (Dionysius, Appian, Dio), but the casus belli is secure. In 281 the consul L. Aemilius Barbula ravaged Tarentine territory, and the Tarentines invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, who had earlier received Tarentine help.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

events.title: Tarentum invites Pyrrhus
events.summary: Facing the consul L. Aemilius Barbula's army, Tarentum and its Italian allies invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, offering a combined force of 350,000 foot and 20,000 horse (a boast); Pyrrhus sent Milo ahead with 3,000 men to garrison the citadel.
events.detail: Pyrrhus, recently expelled from Macedon and seeking a western empire, obtained ships from Antigonus Gonatas, money from Antiochus I and 5,000 Macedonian infantry plus elephants on loan from Ptolemy Keraunos for two years. Plutarch's dialogue between Pyrrhus and Cineas ('and then we shall rest') dates from this moment.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Garoufalias, Pyrrhus, King of Epirus (1979)

events.title: The Campanian legion seizes Rhegium
events.summary: A Roman garrison of 4,000 Campanian citizen-soldiers under Decius Vibellius, sent to protect Rhegium against Pyrrhus, imitated the Mamertines across the strait, massacred or expelled the men and took the city for themselves.
events.detail: Rome could do nothing during the Pyrrhic War; the city was recaptured in 270.

events.title: Battle of Heraclea
events.summary: Pyrrhus defeated the consul P. Valerius Laevinus on the plain between Heraclea and Pandosia by the river Siris; the Roman cavalry and legions held the phalanx through seven charges until Pyrrhus' 20 elephants, never seen before by Romans, panicked the horses.
events.detail: Pyrrhus was nearly killed, having exchanged armour with his companion Megacles, who fell. Losses: Hieronymus of Cardia (via Plutarch) gives 7,000 Romans and just under 4,000 Pyrrhic dead; Dionysius gives 15,000 and 13,000. Lucanians, Bruttians, Messapians and Greek cities joined Pyrrhus; Locri expelled its Roman garrison. The Romans called the elephants 'Lucanian oxen' (boves Lucae). Pyrrhus was impressed by the Roman camp and order ('the discipline of these barbarians is not barbarous').
events.locName: Plain of the Siris near Heraclea (Policoro)

sides.strength: c. 25,000-30,000 including 20 elephants, Macedonian phalanx, Thessalian cavalry, Tarentines

battle.significance: First clash of legion and Hellenistic phalanx; first Roman encounter with war elephants.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 317-340
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

events.title: Pyrrhus marches on Rome
events.summary: After Heraclea, Pyrrhus advanced through Campania (failing to take Capua and Neapolis) up the Via Latina to Anagnia or Praeneste, perhaps within 60 km of Rome, but finding Laevinus reinforced and Coruncanius' army back from Etruria, he withdrew to winter in Tarentum.
events.detail: Plutarch says he came within 300 stades (c. 55 km) of Rome; Eutropius has him reach Praeneste. No Latin colony or ally defected, the first demonstration that Rome's Italian system held under pressure.

events.title: Cineas' embassy and the speech of Appius Claudius
events.summary: Pyrrhus sent his Thessalian orator Cineas to Rome with gifts and offers of peace if Rome left the Italiote Greeks free; as the Senate wavered, the old, blind Appius Claudius Caecus had himself carried to the Curia and declared Rome would not negotiate while a foreign army stood in Italy.
events.detail: Cicero knew a written version of the speech, the earliest Roman oration preserved in his day, and Ennius versified it ('quo vobis mentes, rectae quae stare solebant antehac, dementes sese flexere viai?'). Cineas reported that the Senate seemed to him an assembly of kings and that fighting Rome was like fighting a hydra. Fabricius led a counter-embassy about prisoners, refusing Pyrrhus' gifts; Pyrrhus released prisoners on parole for the Saturnalia, and all returned. Chronology (280 or 279) is debated.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
events.debate: Date and sequence of embassies (280 or after Ausculum in 279).

events.title: Battle of Ausculum
events.summary: Pyrrhus fought the consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus over two days in rough ground near Ausculum in Apulia; on the second day he forced a battle on the plain and won, but at such cost that he reportedly said 'one more such victory and we are finished', the origin of 'Pyrrhic victory'.
events.detail: Hieronymus (via Plutarch) gives 6,000 Roman and 3,505 Pyrrhic dead; Dionysius gives a detailed order of battle with Italian and Greek contingents. Romans used anti-elephant wagons with spikes and fire-pots. A tradition (Cicero) has the third Decius Mus devote himself like his father and grandfather; Zonaras says Pyrrhus warned the Romans he would take Decius alive, and other sources say he survived. Pyrrhus was wounded by a javelin.

sides.strength: four legions plus allies, c. 40,000 (consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus)

battle.significance: The proverbial 'Pyrrhic victory'; Pyrrhus turns to Sicily.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 370-392
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
events.debate: Third Decian devotio; outcome (Roman sources claim a draw or victory).

events.title: Fourth treaty between Rome and Carthage (against Pyrrhus)
events.summary: A Carthaginian admiral, Mago, arrived at Ostia with 120 ships to offer help; the resulting treaty, quoted by Polybius, renewed the earlier ones and provided that if either made an alliance with Pyrrhus it should reserve the right to help the other, with Carthage supplying ships for transport and combat but no obligation for crews to fight on land against their will.
events.detail: The Senate declined immediate naval help (Justin), but the treaty kept Rome and Carthage aligned while Pyrrhus turned to Sicily. A Carthaginian fleet ferried 500 Romans to Rhegium and burned timber Pyrrhus had collected.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 349-351
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998)

events.title: Fabricius returns Pyrrhus' would-be poisoner
events.summary: Pyrrhus' physician (named Nicias or Cineas in some sources) offered the consul Fabricius to poison the king; Fabricius sent him back to Pyrrhus with a letter, and Pyrrhus released his Roman prisoners without ransom.
events.detail: An exemplum of Roman fides retold endlessly (Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Plutarch, Gellius citing Claudius Quadrigarius' text of the letter). It eased negotiations before Pyrrhus departed for Sicily.

events.title: Pyrrhus crosses to Sicily
events.summary: Invited by Syracuse, Acragas and Leontini against Carthage, which was besieging Syracuse, Pyrrhus left Milo in Tarentum and sailed with c. 8,000 foot and elephants from Locri to Tauromenium and Catana, lifted the siege of Syracuse and was hailed hegemon and king of Sicily.
events.detail: His claim rested partly on his marriage to Lanassa, daughter of Agathocles, and on his son Alexander, Agathocles' grandson. The Syracusan factions of Thoenon and Sosistratus handed him the city and its fleet of some 120-140 ships.

events.title: Pyrrhus storms Eryx
events.summary: Pyrrhus stormed the Carthaginian mountain stronghold of Eryx, being himself first onto the walls in Homeric style, and celebrated games to Heracles as he had vowed; Panormus also fell.
events.detail: By the end of 277 only Lilybaeum remained in Carthaginian hands. Eryx would later be the scene of Hamilcar Barca's long resistance (244-241).

events.title: Pyrrhus fails before Lilybaeum
events.summary: Carthage, supplied by sea, offered Pyrrhus money and ships for peace; he demanded they evacuate Sicily entirely, then failed in a two-month siege of the impregnable sea-fortress of Lilybaeum.
events.detail: Pyrrhus then planned to invade Africa, demanded rowers and money from the Sicilian Greeks, and executed Thoenon; the cities turned against him, some inviting back the Carthaginians or Mamertines.

battle.significance: Turning point of Pyrrhus' Sicilian venture.

events.title: Naval battle in the Strait of Messina
events.summary: Recalled by his Italian allies, Pyrrhus sailed back to Italy and was attacked in the strait by a Carthaginian fleet, losing many ships; landing, he was harassed by 10,000 Mamertines, then took Locri and plundered the treasury of Persephone to pay his troops.
events.detail: A storm wrecked the ships carrying the temple treasure, which washed up at Locri; Pyrrhus, terrified, restored it (Dionysius, Livy 29.18 for the Locrian tradition). Pyrrhus' parting remark on Sicily, 'what a wrestling ground we leave for Carthaginians and Romans', is recorded by Plutarch.

sides.losses: many ships sunk or disabled (Plutarch: 70 ruined)

events.title: Battle of Beneventum (Maleventum)
events.summary: Pyrrhus attempted a night march to surprise the consul M'. Curius Dentatus near Maleventum, but lost his way in wooded hills and arrived at dawn exhausted; Curius drove back his troops and stampeded elephants into his own lines, and Pyrrhus abandoned Italy.
events.detail: Curius' triumph in 275 featured four captured elephants, the first seen in Rome, and spoils that paid for the Anio Vetus aqueduct. Ancient sources disagree whether it was a decisive defeat (Roman tradition) or a drawn engagement (Plutarch implies a Roman success but not a rout). Maleventum was renamed Beneventum as a better omen when colonised in 268. Pyrrhus left Milo in Tarentum and sailed home with 8,000 foot and 500 horse.

sides.strength: c. 20,000-25,000 with elephants and Samnite allies

battle.significance: Ends Pyrrhus' Italian venture; Rome becomes master of southern Italy.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 505-520
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

events.title: Census of 275 and the expulsion of Rufinus
events.summary: The census of 275 counted 271,224 citizens, down from 287,222 in 280/279; the censor C. Fabricius Luscinus expelled the twice-consul P. Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.
events.detail: Rufinus, a capable general who had taken Croton in 277, was ancestor of Sulla. The anecdote became a staple of Roman moral nostalgia about early austerity, but it also shows that luxury silver was entering Rome with Greek contact.

events.title: Ptolemy II establishes friendship with Rome
events.summary: Impressed by Rome's defeat of Pyrrhus, Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent an embassy to Rome and a treaty of friendship (amicitia) was made; Rome returned an embassy of Q. Fabius Gurges, N. Fabius Pictor and Q. Ogulnius, who refused Ptolemy's personal gifts and deposited them in the treasury.
events.detail: The first formal Roman relationship with a Hellenistic great power. Lycophron's Alexandra, perhaps of these years (or a later interpolation), speaks of the descendants of Aeneas winning 'the sceptre and monarchy of land and sea'.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984) 673-678

events.title: Latin colonies at Paestum and Cosa; Caere punished
events.summary: Rome founded Latin colonies at Paestum (Greek Poseidonia, long ruled by Lucanians) and at Cosa on the Etruscan coast, on territory taken from Vulci; Caere lost half its territory after an abortive revolt.
events.detail: Cosa, excavated by the American Academy (F. E. Brown), is the type-site of the Latin colony: hilltop polygonal walls, grid, forum and Capitolium, harbour below. At Paestum the colonists built a forum and comitium beside the old Greek temples.
scholarship: Brown, Cosa: The Making of a Roman Town (1980)
Fentress (ed.), Cosa V (2003)

events.title: Death of Pyrrhus at Argos
events.summary: After a failed attack on Sparta, Pyrrhus fought his way into Argos at night; in the street fighting an old woman threw a roof tile from a housetop, stunning him, and a soldier of Antigonus Gonatas beheaded him.
events.detail: With Pyrrhus dead, his garrison commander Milo surrendered Tarentum to Rome. Hannibal is said (Plutarch, Livy) to have ranked Pyrrhus first or second among generals. Pyrrhus' own memoirs were used by later historians.

events.title: Surrender of Tarentum
events.summary: Besieged by L. Papirius Cursor and with a Carthaginian fleet appearing off the harbour, Pyrrhus' general Milo surrendered the citadel of Tarentum to Rome in exchange for safe passage; Tarentum's walls were demolished, its ships and arms surrendered, and it became a Roman ally.
events.detail: Whether the Carthaginian fleet came to help Rome (per treaty) or to seize Tarentum itself was later disputed and fed mutual suspicion. Papirius' triumph displayed rich Greek art. Livius Andronicus, the father of Latin literature, was traditionally brought to Rome as a captive from Tarentum at this time. The same year triumphs were celebrated over the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians.

sides.strength: Epirote garrison under Milo and Tarentines

battle.significance: End of the Pyrrhic War; Rome master of Magna Graecia.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)

events.title: Final submission of Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians
events.summary: Campaigns of 273-272 against the peoples who had joined Pyrrhus ended with triumphs over the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians; the Bruttians lost half the Sila forest with its timber and pitch, and the Samnite League was broken up into separate treaty states.
events.detail: Latin colonies at Beneventum (268) and Aesernia (263) were planted in Samnium. The Bruttian loss of the Sila forest gave Rome shipbuilding timber and pitch just before the First Punic War.

events.title: Construction of the Anio Vetus aqueduct
events.summary: The censors M'. Curius Dentatus and L. Papirius Praetextatus let the contract for Rome's second aqueduct, financed from the spoils of Pyrrhus, drawing water from the Anio above Tibur along a winding course of 43 Roman miles (c. 64 km), almost all underground.
events.detail: Curius died before completion, and the Senate appointed duumviri aquae perducendae (Curius and Fulvius Flaccus) to finish it. Frontinus records its daily discharge as 4,398 quinariae, more than double the Aqua Appia, though its water was turbid and later used for gardens and baths.
scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)

events.title: Recapture of Rhegium and punishment of the Campanian legion
events.summary: Rome, with grain and troops supplied by Hiero of Syracuse, besieged and stormed Rhegium; the 300 surviving mutineers of the Campanian legion were taken to Rome, flogged and beheaded in the Forum in batches of fifty, and the city was restored to the surviving Rhegines.
events.detail: Polybius stresses that Rome thereby demonstrated fides to its allies. The contrast with Rome's acceptance of the Mamertines' similar crime six years later was noted by Polybius as Rome's embarrassment in 264.

sides.strength: consular army (Cn. Cornelius Blasio?) with Syracusan supplies
Campanian legion, c. 4,000 at the outset

battle.significance: Rome shows fides to Greek allies; cooperation with Hiero.

events.title: Battle of the Longanus river; Hiero becomes king
events.summary: Hiero, general of Syracuse, decisively defeated the Mamertines on the Longanus river near Mylae, captured their leaders, and was acclaimed king (basileus) by the Syracusans; the Mamertines appealed for help, first to a Carthaginian garrison and then to Rome.
events.detail: The date is disputed: Polybius' narrative implies c. 269 (before Hiero's 54-year reign ending in 215, i.e. accession 270/269), while others place the battle in 265/264 immediately before the Mamertine appeal. Polybius praises Hiero's careful policy, and his long reign as a loyal Roman ally after 263.

battle.significance: Hiero becomes king; Mamertine appeals lead to the First Punic War.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 54-55
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998) 33-46
tags: road to the First Punic War

events.title: First Roman silver coinage at Rome (Pliny's 269)
events.summary: Pliny says the Roman people first struck silver in 269, five years before the First Punic War; numismatists reinterpret this as the didrachm with Hercules / she-wolf and twins and the legend ROMANO, among the Romano-Campanian series, rather than the denarius (introduced c. 211).
events.detail: The she-wolf didrachm echoes the Ogulnian monument of 296. Romano-Campanian silver was probably struck at Neapolis or Rome itself for payments in the south and Sicily.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) 39-41
Burnett, 'The beginnings of Roman coinage', AIIN 36 (1989)

events.title: Conquest of Picenum: battle during an earthquake
events.summary: The consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and Ap. Claudius Russus defeated the Picentes near Asculum (Ascoli Piceno); when an earthquake shook the field, Sempronius vowed a temple to Tellus (Earth), and the battle was won.
events.detail: Part of the Picentes were deported to the Gulf of Salerno, around Picentia. The temple of Tellus on the Carinae was built on the site of Sp. Cassius' razed house.

events.title: Latin colonies at Ariminum and Beneventum; Sabines enfranchised
events.summary: Ariminum (Rimini) on the Adriatic, Rome's northern bastion against the Gauls of the Po valley, and Beneventum, renamed from Maleventum, in the heart of Samnium, became Latin colonies; the Sabines received full citizenship.
events.detail: Ariminum, later terminus of the Via Flaminia (220), was the leading Latin colony of the north and in 209 was among the eighteen colonies that stayed loyal when twelve refused troops. Cicero's 'ius duodecim coloniarum' (Pro Caecina 102), a restricted form of Latin rights, is associated with Ariminum and the colonies founded after it.

events.title: Quaestors increased to eight; Sallentine war
events.summary: The number of quaestors was doubled to eight, the new 'quaestores classici' (or Italici) stationed in Italy, at Ostia, Cales and elsewhere, to manage fleet levies and relations with the allies; the same year Rome campaigned against the Sallentini and Messapians whose chief port, Brundisium, came under Roman control.
events.detail: The new quaestors reflect the administrative demands of Roman Italy just before the First Punic War: naval contributions of the Greek allies (socii navales) and coastal defence. Triumphs over the Sallentini were celebrated in 267 and 266.
scholarship: Harris, 'The development of the quaestorship 267-81 BC', CQ 26 (1976)
events.debate: Precise functions and seats of the quaestores classici.

events.title: Rome hands over young nobles who struck the envoys of Apollonia
events.summary: Two young Romans of senatorial family, Q. Fabius and Cn. Apronius, insulted and struck envoys from Apollonia in Illyria; the Senate handed them over to the Apolloniates, who released them unharmed.
events.detail: The episode is evidence of Roman contact across the Adriatic decades before the Illyrian war of 229 and of Roman concern for the sanctity of envoys.

events.title: Subjugation of the Umbrian Sarsinates
events.summary: The consuls of 266 celebrated triumphs over the Sarsinates of the upper Savio valley (birthplace of Plautus), completing the reduction of Umbria.
events.detail: With the Sallentini and Picentes subdued, all of peninsular Italy south of the Arno-Rubicon line was now under Roman control or alliance.

events.title: Destruction of Volsinii
events.summary: The aristocrats of Volsinii, overthrown by their freedmen or slaves who had taken power, appealed to Rome; M. Fulvius Flaccus besieged and took the city, razed it, moved the population to a new site by Lake Bolsena, and carried off some 2,000 bronze statues.
events.detail: Fulvius triumphed on 1 November 264. A dedication by M. Fulvius at the sanctuary of S. Omobono in Rome was found in the 1960s, and he may have 'evoked' the Volsinian god Vertumnus (Voltumna) to a temple on the Aventine. Volsinii (Etruscan Velzna, modern Orvieto) was the site of the federal sanctuary of the Etruscans, the Fanum Voltumnae, now located at Campo della Fiera below Orvieto. Pliny says the statues were the real motive for the war.

sides.strength: consular army of M. Fulvius Flaccus
sides.losses: consul Q. Fabius Gurges died of wounds in 265

sides.strength: city held by former slaves or freedmen

battle.significance: End of Etruscan independence; transfer of the Fanum Voltumnae's prestige to Rome.

scholarship: Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971) 115-118
Stopponi, 'Campo della Fiera at Orvieto: new discoveries', in Turfa (ed.), The Etruscan World (2013)

events.title: Census of 265: 292,234 citizens; ban on iterating the censorship
events.summary: The lustrum of 265 counted 292,234 citizens; C. Marcius Rutilus, censor for the second time, rebuked the people for re-electing him and carried a law forbidding anyone to hold the censorship twice, earning the cognomen Censorinus.
events.detail: The figure, on the eve of the First Punic War, gives the Roman citizen manpower that would man the first fleets of 260. The rule against iteration held for the rest of the Republic.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 BC - AD 14 (1971) 13
